newsitem.title: UK: British industry grows for 11th month in a row.
newsitem.headline: British industry grows for 11th month in a row.

text.p: British manufacturing industry expanded in April for the 11th month in a row as good domestic demand offset the damaging impact on exports of the strong pound, according to a leading business survey on Thursday.
The purchasing managers' index (PMI), published by the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply as voting got underway in Britain's general election, rose to 53.1 in April from 52.8 in March.
"Companies continued to raise output to meet further improvements in order books," the institute said in its Report on Business.

"Although the rate of growth of export orders again declined as a result of the sustained strength of the pound in April, any losses were largely offset by the continued buoyancy of demand for manufactured goods from domestic customers."
The survey, sponsored by Reuters, confirmed that the economy was in a fairly healthy state, with steady growth, falling unemployment and low inflation.

But opinion polls suggested Prime Minister John Major's Conservative government was unlikely to be given credit by voters for the recovery. Final polls pointed to a win for Tony Blair's opposition Labour party.

Economists said the survey showed manufacturing industry remained vulnerable and could suffer if, as widely expected, interest rates are raised soon after the election to prevent a resurgence of inflation.
"With the full effect of the pound's rise yet to become clear, it is far too soon to conclude that manufacturers have escaped unscathed," said Jonathan Loynes. an economist at HSBC Markets.
"Industry needs a sharp post-election rise in interest rates -- and the further rise in the pound it could precipitate -- like a hole in the head."

Economists Simon Briscoe and Edmund Nonis of Nikko Europe said the strong pound was clearly hurting manufacturers. They argued that the next government should raise taxes rather than interest rates to help curb demand without boosting sterling.
"The strength of sterling is a double-sided coin, acting to keep pipeline inflationary pressures subdued," they wrote in a comment on the PMI survey.
"The weakness of the manufacturing sector continues to argue for tighter fiscal policy as the preferred policy tool in place of higher interest rates."

The survey showed overall growth in new orders remained strong, although it was lower than that recorded in the second half of 1996, before the appreciation in sterling began to subdue demand for exports.
"Order levels have now risen for 11 consecutive months," the CIPS said.

High sales levels depleted stocks of finished goods for the second month running. "However, significant capacity pressures -- and the potential inflationary impact of supply shortages -- have yet to appear."
With spare capacity in many sectors, more purchasing managers negotiated lower prices than faced price rises from suppliers.
The continued strength of sterling dampened export demand to some extent but also reduced the cost of imported goods.
"Restructuring to improve competitiveness remains commonplace and manufacturing employment expanded only slightly as a result in April," the survey said.
